In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks.

The significant discrepancy between advancing computational technology and real-world problem-solving led to a new field of study. Abramson and Parashar suggest that a parallel disparity in complex software and challenging practical applications calls for the emergence of translational computer science. From this viewpoint, we reexamine the development and deployment of grid computing. A translational perspective is helpful for comprehending the progress of grid computing technology. Specifically, we show how developing the grid computing infrastructure and its management system can be seen as an example of applying TCSC principles to bridge the development phase and production deployment, resulting in an efficient and scalable solution.

A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous components. This model has the ability to smoothly transition between the equations of state for dark energy and dust at different cosmological epochs, by asymptotically interpolating between two power laws. A constant viscosity coefficient underlies the model's dissipative component. Using a phase space analysis, we investigate the model's dynamics in a framework that is robust and solution-independent. Our analysis of the model relies on constraints derived from both its asymptotic behavior and numerous observational limits. Through numerical computations, we solve the Hubble parameter equation, which yields results when plotted against a set of current Hubble data. Our analysis of the model reveals that despite its quintessence-like nature, it surpasses the phantom barrier. To assess the model's predictions for the universe's evolution, we investigate the development of both the deceleration and qc parameters, as well as the scale factor. Our findings for the model's dissipative component align with current constraints, and the associated dark energy parameter falls within the interval [0.10, 0.30]. This broadens upon the typical values reported in other models. Furthermore, our analysis of the statefinders reveals that the model is capable of replicating the observed features of the universe's evolution. Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting likelihood fits for individual neutrino and dark matter operators with varying Lorentz structures and photon spectrums. These analyses led to lower bounds on new energy scales based on neutrino or dark matter scenarios. Specifically, the most stringent limits on energy scales were found to be 12.8 GeV for neutrinos and 11.6 GeV for dark matter within their respective effective field theories. We also found that J/ψ decay into purely invisible matter imposes additional constraints on certain effective operators, with energy scales above 100 GeV for dipole operators. Moreover, our study revealed that J/ψ invisible decays can be sensitive to light dark matter mass ranges inaccessible to direct detection experiments, with future facilities such as the Super Tau Charm Factory having the potential to discover dark matter within these intervals.

This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a comprehensive framework consisting of theoretical underpinnings and a step-by-step implementation guide for the algorithm. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of MFSSA through comparative studies of reconstruction accuracy in multivariate functional time series (MFTS) and real-world applications, including the analysis of intraday temperature curves and remote sensing images of vegetation. Additionally, MFSSA is made available through the Rfssa R package for user convenience.

The power law decay $p(t,x) \sim t^{-\phi(x,b)/2}$ holds, where $p(t,x)$ is the probability that, during the interval $[1,t]$, the random walk $S$ with zero-mean increments has spent a fraction of time greater than $x$ with non-negative values, occurring for a walk that is defined by finitely many i.i.d. increment values. The parameter $\phi(x,b)$ is determined by the probability $\mathbb{P}(\text{L\'evy}(1/2,\kappa(x,b))<0)$ where $\kappa(x,b) = \frac{\sqrt{1-x}b-\sqrt{1+x}}{\sqrt{1-x}b+\sqrt{1+x}}$ with $b = b_S \geq 0$ indicating the relative magnitude between positive and negative excursions of the random walk.

The Helicon Endplate Plasma Source (HEPS) is a type of plasma source 
that benefits from its large size, which gives it high power handling 
capabilities and a large plasma volume.  To take advantage of these 
features fully, it is crucial to achieve discharge in the helicon mode, 
which can be done by tuning matching networks and ensuring sufficient 
frequency and gas pressure conditions.  This study presents HEPS, 
modified to reach the helicon mode of discharge.  Key modifications 
included adding a second quarter-wavelength transmission line to the 
helicon heater's matching network and installing a hollow waveguide 
inside HEPS to allow for extensive plasma extent along its axis.  This 
achievement was confirmed using Langmuir probes and spectrometer 
diagnostics.  This development marks an important step in preparing 
HEPS for its primary purpose of miniaturized helium-2 plasma 
thruster testing.

While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort. To streamline this process, a common strategy involves using nucleus segmentation to calculate features that can classify images as cancerous or not. However, training a nucleus segmentation model is challenging due to the extensive variation in the appearance of nuclei in cancerous images. To address this issue, we propose incorporating a style transfer algorithm, specifically StyleGAN, into our segmentation framework. During training, the model receives both the input image and a randomly selected style, allowing the network to extract content while preserving the target style, thus mimicking the desired characteristics. Experimental results demonstrate that utilizing style transfer leads to improved performance compared to using only content.

Let's consider a non-Archimedean local field of characteristic not two and denote it by F. Additionally, let G be either a specific type of special orthogonal group with an odd number of dimensions or a symplectic group with a specific dimensionality, denoted as SO(2r+1)(F) or Sp(2r)(F) respectively. This paper focuses on establishing the local converse theorem for the representation of G. To this end, for two given irreducible admissible generic representations of G, with shared central character and gamma factors, our result stipulates that these representations are isomorphic. To prove this, we draw from the Cogdell, Shahidi, and Tsai framework of partial Bessel functions and the categorization of irreducible generic representations. Furthermore, our result extends the earlier works by Jiang and Soudry as well as Q. Zhang, by expanding on their results for the cases with supercuspidal representations in a wider set of characteristic settings.

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex, high-dimensional data patterns, despite the computational demands of some GCNN components. A significant portion of the input data in GCNNs can be redundant, prompting an interest in achieving a balance between efficiency and accuracy by eliminating unnecessary connections. Graph convolutional layers, the core of many GCNN designs, are particularly suited for generalization to unseen data but are heavily dependent on connectivity patterns. This research introduces a novel approach to enhance the efficiency of GCNNs, called BitMask, which determines binary selections to remove unnecessary connections from GCNN architectures, directly from training data without requiring manual problem-specific knowledge. BitMask evaluates the importance of nodes within individual samples and uses this to create data-specific graphs for training, effectively improving the performance of the resulting GCNN while reducing computational requirements. Experimental results on various class-division patterns and complex datasets like CIFAR-10 and 20 demonstrate that BitMask can identify and eliminate highly redundant connections while maintaining GCNN accuracy and offering insights into the inherent sparsity of effective neural network structures.

In a three-dimensional spacetime, Einstein's gravity theory is transformed to represent a scalar field with a complex, self-correcting mechanism. The field's behavior can be reinterpreted using Chern-Simons form for a pair of conformally coupled massless theories that split into distinct self-dual and anti-self-dual components. The self-dual and anti-self-dual theories, denoted as $f$ and $\bar{f}$, share the same form but adopt different star product definitions. The soliton solution for the coupled equations, known as the Baekler soliton, arises when the connection has a non-trivial holonomy. The condition of trivial holonomy is naturally met when the cosmological constant is very large, but this also occurs for mixed states of the $f$ and $\bar{f}$ theories without a holographic stress-energy tensor. The absence of this tensor implies the trivial holonomy condition is not arbitrary, but rather a necessary constraint. The set of allowed gauge fields, called the algebra of deformations, results in a closed structure under multiplication but lacks inverses, making it quasi-Bernoulli. The Baekler soliton exists as an isolated, exceptional solution within this framework.

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the visual inspection and tactile assessment of tissue stiffness, a crucial characteristic, via ultrasound.  A key hindrance to high-quality elastography images is the low signal-to-noise ratio associated with ultrasound speckle.  Synthetic aperture (SA) imaging, a method that combines recorded echoes to create images with enhanced lateral resolution and reduced noise, has shown improvement in elastography by synthesizing high-quality elasticity images.  However, the SA method also synthesizes compounded received signals with varying phases of axial compression, distorting the elasticity image.  The proposed Virtual Source Synthetic Aperture (VSSA) method overcomes this challenge by synthesizing images with improved lateral resolution and reduced noise, while maintaining the original waveforms at the transducer source to preserve the compression elasticity map.  Simulations and experimental data from in-vivo supraspinatus muscle images have shown that the VSSA method with 4 and 12 transducer elements provides improved elasticity images with better lateral resolution, reduced noise, and higher quality elastograms, in comparison with the conventional full-width elastograms.

Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an innovative perspective, which we can view as a modern interpretation of the computability logic framework. Specifically, it aligns with the approach of MC^2 computability logic, which we can understand as a development of that framework without the need for abstract assumptions. This needlessness is achieved by representing the problem to be solved and the solution to be executed as components of a single, cohesive system.

In the context of dynamic data streams, where Euclidean space points are added or removed from a dataset, we develop a one-pass algorithm for solving the $k$-means clustering problem. This algorithm's time complexity is directly proportional to the dimensionality of the space and square root of the number of clusters, with a stream complexity that highlights a logarithmic factor related to the desired accuracy and another term that represents the number of updates per unit of stream data. Our solution improves upon the time complexity of existing methods and achieves a significant enhancement in space complexity, which we prove is optimal to within a constant factor for a specific range of parameters. Additionally, our approach is continuous, implying that the resulting centroid locations can be maintained with limited precision, despite the stream containing approximate data points.

We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing the outcome values of the individual games as rewards in the aggregated framework. Through extensive simulations, our hierarchical model demonstrates substantial computational efficiency improvements while achieving comparable performance to flat Nash policies.

Due to the tendency for high-energy lepton colliders to radiate forward and resemble weak boson colliders beyond a few TeV, a new perspective is taken that treats weak bosons as fundamental components of these processes. Using this weak boson collener approach, the real emission of photons and W/Z bosons, along with hadrons in processes involving W/Z fusion, are calculated to NLO accuracy within the W-boson collinear framework. A detailed analysis of phase space limitations, matrix elements, and suppression factors is also conducted. An investigation into the W-boson collinear approach's limitations, an explanation of the associated collinear divergences and their matching to parton distribution functions (PDFs) in both $\mathcal{O}(\alpha_s)$ and $\mathcal{O}(\alpha_{\rm QED})$ orders is also carried out. An assessment of the NLO W-boson collinear factorization scheme is performed, an estimate of the relevant hadronic uncertainty is performed, and an update to the EW W-boson PDF is also done within the W-boson collinear scheme for the CT18 parton set. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios.

We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser from 1936, whose respective proofs show striking similarities and utilize the same fundamental techniques.

This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space.

In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. We developed a method to generate a multitude of high-quality samples per second from the posterior distribution by using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which outperformed current methods according to Fr\'{e}chet inception distance metrics in applications like MRI with multiple coils and image inpainting.

This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions for specific invariant configurations in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. We also discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds.

The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's performance in speech synthesis.

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence.

Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the sound source object, and easier elements, including those that do not include the source object. By sorting the video features into harder and easier samples and then focusing on harder samples, our method achieves better results. To accomplish this, we introduce a difficulty classification module that distingu between difficult and easy samples, and a difficulty re-mining module to select the hardest samples for loss function optimization. Our experiments on public datasets demonstrate that this approach significantly boosts accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods.

Recent advancements in graph embedding have been focused on preserving various properties of scale-free and hierarchical graphs in lower-dimensional spaces, particularly within the framework of hyperbolic geometry. However, these approaches struggle to directly preserve the branching structure of trees and hierarchical graphs by failing to account for key parameters in the Lorentzian metric that define this structure. This study proposes a novel hyperbolic embedding method under the Lorentzian metric designed to preserve tree branching factors. Theory and simulations demonstrate that this approach is mathematically consistent with the Mauldin-Williams tree model, a common framework for analyzing randomly generated infinite trees. Furthermore, we develop a practical algorithm for embedding finite trees and evaluate its performance using synthetic data, showing significant improvements over existing methods in tasks such as link prediction and graph task classification based on tree properties.

This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequality and a compactness-uniqueness argument. An operator theoretical approach provides the regularity needed for initial conditions, thereby obtaining the desired stability estimate.

We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating
variations in impulsivity, which is analogous to the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting
model proposed by Takahashi, with a dual nature. We show that our model's
parameters correlate with the average and standard deviation of impulsivity, and
these results provide a clear path for investigating the Tsallis distribution in a
social context.

When considering linearized gravity within a harmonic gauge theory for a symmetric tensor field, implementing the harmonic gauge yields multiple gauge options, resulting in the gauge appearing as a class rather than a singular choice.  This feature provides a physical justification for adopting a specific covariant harmonic gauge that arises when a mass term is added to the gravitational perturbation.  Specifically, one particular choice of harmonic gauge leads to a linearized massive gravity model with the correct five degrees of freedom and avoids the vDVZ discontinuity, in contrast to the standard Fierz-Pauli theory.

For a class of quadratic Hamiltonians, a transformation of Weyl-Wigner symbols through a change of variables reveals the canonical thermal equilibrium quantum states, using the Weyl-Wigner representations and metaplectic operators, whose associated unitary classical structures behave predictably under the transform, exposing the complex symplectic matrix that dictates the entire thermal equilibrium state and thereby determines its thermal properties. Additionally, a thorough examination is performed of four distinct types of Hamiltonian dynamics: parabolic, elliptic, hyperbolic, and loxodromic dynamics. Semiclassical and high-temperature approximations are both determined and contrasted to their respective classical or quadratic behaviors.

The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both mathematical and graphical means, specifically in the context of a two-level system. We contend that the simplicity of these calculations can offer undergraduates a clear, tangible understanding of temperatures below zero.

Within the simplest scoto-seesaw model, we examine the consistency between the electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino characteristics, and dark matter behavior. By integrating the minimal dark sector into the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw framework, we establish a comprehensive understanding of neutrino oscillation lengths. Here, the "atmospheric" mass scale is directly proportional to the ratio of the vacuum expectation value squared to the dark matter mass times the coupling constant, while the "solar" scale depends on additional model parameters. Furthermore, we determine the dark energy scale as well. Through a detailed analysis of the neutrino mass matrix, we derive constraints on model parameters from experimental data, allowing us to explore the parameter space for symmetry breaking, neutrino oscillations, and dark matter. By iterating through different scenarios, we establish correlations between model parameters and establish the relationship between the "atmospheric" mass scale and the dark matter abundance. Ultimately, we determine the predicted thermal relic abundance, extra thermal corrections, neutrino oscillation lengths, and dark matter direct detection cross-sections.

We employ exact diagonalization to examine the effects of spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions on the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ $d$-orbital states in a cubic crystal structure, characteristic of transition metal oxides. By directly comparing with $t_{2g}$ only or $e_g$ only models based on electron filling, we determine the branching ratio for magnetic ordering temperatures and average moments for $d^4$ to $d^7$ configurations. Our findings reveal that $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing, influenced by interactions and crystal field splitting, can result in magnetic moments interpreting experimental data with an incorrect orbital assignment. Notably, we observe that the average moment does not monotonically change with electron filling due to $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing, and we find that $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ orbitals are equally occupied in the $d^6$ case with significant spin-orbit coupling and uranium compounds.

This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through analytical means. Furthermore, it explores connections between these results and the related mathematical theories of extremal transitions and FJRW.

Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in image editing has emerged, utilizing a style-based chest X-ray generator. This innovation enables the transfer of anatomical and stylistic attributes between images, allowing for the absorption of medical knowledge from data and the generation of styled X-rays for training purposes without compromising authenticity. By analyzing implicit features within latent codes, a style-based approach was found to be more effective than the style transfer style. Additionally, a medical knowledge absorption mechanism was developed, categorizing features into discriminative and enveloping portions, with the assumption that the latter contains stylistic information. This mechanism creates multiple domain-adapted latent codes by combining the former portion of the original code with varied stylistic portions of the replacement code. The resulting results showcase successful feature manipulation and a capacity to generate multi-styled latent codes. The absorption mechanism also demonstrates the ability to adapt to diverse medical data with distinct distributions. Furthermore, evaluations utilizing real-world datasets highlight a style-based domain adaptation that preserves natural authenticity while conferring a stylistic characteristic. The paper also exposes an unexpected correlation between a specific subset of latent dimensions and pathological information, as well as the integration of external medical data through latent code manipulation.

ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and
advanced analysis. It is capable of handling object-feature tables that include
numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool
encompasses several statistical techniques such as weighted PCA, elastic maps,
linear discriminant analysis, and decision tree construction, in addition to
K-Means clustering and multilinear regression. With customizable visualizations
and an interactive 3D viewer, ViDaExpert enables the creation of 3D scenes
from data and facilitates rapid, in-depth analysis of data, encompassing
elementary to complex methodologies.
